strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: there is no standardized benchmark for memory in robotic manipulation RL, and the paper makes a convincing case via Table 2/Table 3 that existing memory benchmarks (POPGym, DMLab, Memory Maze, etc.) are abstract/navigation-focused and that robotics frameworks largely lack memory-intensive tasks.

MIKASA-Robo is a substantial and concrete contribution: 32 tabletop manipulation tasks across 12 categories with multiple difficulty modes, built on ManiSkill3 with GPU-parallel training, multiple observation modes (state/RGB/joints), and both dense and sparse reward variants. Detailed per-task documentation in Appendix E supports reproducibility.

Good benchmark hygiene: the authors validate solvability of all tasks via PPO-MLP with full state (100% success rate), separating task-design flaws from memory/algorithmic limitations; baselines are run with 3 training seeds and 16 evaluation seeds with SEM reported.

The experiments sensibly demonstrate the benchmark's discriminative power in the dense-reward regime: a clear MLP-vs-LSTM gap and progressive degradation with task complexity (e.g., RememberColor 3/5/9) showing the tasks stress memory rather than control skill alone.

MIKASA-Base provides a useful curation service, unifying existing memory environments under the Gymnasium API with a two-tier (diagnostic/complex) structure, which will ease cross-paper comparison even if it is not novel in itself.
weaknesses: Baselines are far too limited to substantiate the central claim of enabling 'objective evaluation of memory mechanisms across different agents'. Only PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM are tested; no transformer/state-space-based memory architectures (GTrXL, R2I, AMAGO, HCAM, etc.) that the paper itself lists as the main memory-enhanced agents. As a result, the benchmark's ability to discriminate among modern memory mechanisms is unproven.

The four-way taxonomy (object/spatial/sequential/capacity) is the first claimed contribution, but it is justified mostly by analogy to cognitive science and appears ad hoc in places: several tasks in Table 5 span multiple categories (e.g., 'Sequential, Object', 'Capacity, Spatial'), and there is no experiment showing that performance across the four categories actually decorrelates across architectures — which is the motivating claim in Figure 1.

Sparse-reward results (Figure 9) show near-zero success for all agents on essentially all tasks, which suggests saturation in difficulty or reward-design problems rather than graded memory evaluation; the benchmark's discriminative value in its most 'realistic' configuration is therefore questionable and under-analyzed.

MIKASA-Base is largely a repackaging and selection of existing open-source environments; the paper presents no baseline results on MIKASA-Base tasks, so this contribution is a curation claim rather than an empirically validated one.

The paper claims tasks 'isolate and evaluate specific memory-dependent skills', but confounds remain: e.g., Intercept/InterceptGrab may be partially solvable reactively from recent frames (velocity estimation from a short window), and the dense-reward shaping (distance-based terms) could allow memory-free agents to exploit progress signals — an isolation analysis is not provided.

Polish issues: the abstract is truncated ('The code is available a'), several typos remain ('panda-gym (Gallouedec´...)', 'am ordered sequence'), and the coverage of results is uneven — many MIKASA-Robo tasks are only characterized in the appendix while the main text leans on a few exemplar tasks.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: no existing benchmark specifically targets memory in robotic tabletop manipulation, and the MIKASA-Robo tasks (32 tasks across 12 categories) are plausibly designed and well-documented with detailed per-task descriptions, reward structures, and success criteria (Appendix E).

Good engineering and reproducibility practices: Gymnasium/ManiSkill3-based implementation, debug wrappers, example code, and stated availability of code; state-mode experiments validating 100% solvability is a useful sanity check.

Useful aggregation work: Table 2 (mapping memory benchmarks to the papers that introduced them) and Table 3 (surveying robotics frameworks for memory-task support) provide helpful overviews for the community.
The diagnostic/complex two-tier structure and separation of dense/sparse reward modes is a sensible benchmark design principle.
weaknesses: Insufficient baseline evaluation to support the central claims. Only PPO-MLP (memory-less) and PPO-LSTM are evaluated. Given that the paper's stated motivation (Figure 1) is that existing benchmarks cannot distinguish between memory mechanisms, the paper provides no evidence that MIKASA can: no transformer-based, state-space-model, or retrieval-based agents (e.g., GTrXL, R2D2, AMAGO, RATE, R2I) are tested. Showing LSTM fails is not enough to demonstrate discriminative power between memory architectures.

The benchmark may be miscalibrated in difficulty. Under the standard RGB+joints mode, even LSTM fails on most tasks, and under sparse rewards both architectures achieve near-zero success everywhere. A benchmark where nearly all current memory-based baselines score ~0% offers little signal for measuring progress and cannot meaningfully rank mechanisms. No difficulty-tuning or curriculum analysis is provided.

The proposed four-category taxonomy (object/spatial/sequential/capacity memory) is asserted rather than validated. No experiment demonstrates that performance profiles actually cluster by these categories, i.e., that the taxonomy has empirical predictive value; the categorization of individual tasks (e.g., classifying Intercept as purely 'spatial') is subjective and not defended.

Limited novelty of MIKASA-Base: it is essentially a curated re-release of existing open-source environments (POPGym, BSuite, Memory Maze, MemoryGym, etc.) under the Gymnasium API. The 'systematic analysis' underlying environment selection is not described as a formal procedure, and Table 4's recommendations are ad hoc.

Experiments use only three training runs per task; for a benchmark paper whose main empirical contribution is validating difficulty, this is thin, especially given the high variance visible in several plots.

Positioning and claims are overblown: the paper repeatedly invokes 'real-world applications' while all tasks are simulated tabletop scenes, and the abstract's truncated final sentence ('The code is available a') and multiple typos (e.g., 'practically simple classification' phrasing, 'the agent does not observes') indicate careless preparation.

Several key design choices are under-specified: how the oracle-info column was derived, whether dense reward components could leak memory (e.g., next-target-cube rewards in capacity tasks), and how prompts are represented for the Rotate tasks.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: there is indeed no standardized benchmark for memory in RL, and especially none for memory-intensive robotic tabletop manipulation; the MIKASA-Robo suite of 32 tasks across 12 categories is a concrete and potentially useful community resource.

The proposed four-category taxonomy (object, spatial, sequential, memory capacity) is grounded in cognitive science literature and provides a practical, easy-to-apply lens for categorizing memory tasks; Table 5's classification of many existing environments demonstrates its applicability.

Careful benchmark validation methodology: demonstrating 100% success rate with PPO-MLP in state mode establishes that tasks are solvable and that failures in RGB+joints mode are attributable to memory/learning limitations rather than task design flaws. The MLP vs. LSTM comparison cleanly shows the benchmark separates memory-less from memory-enhanced agents.

Extensive documentation: detailed per-task descriptions (objectives, phases, success criteria, reward structure), multiple observation modes, Gymnasium API compatibility, debug wrappers, and example code support reproducibility and usability.
Complementary dense/sparse reward settings are a sensible design, and the reporting of both mean ± SEM over three runs with 16 evaluation seeds is methodologically reasonable.

Related work coverage is thorough, including a useful summary table (Table 2) of which memory environments were used by which prior agents, which convincingly motivates the fragmented-evaluation argument.
weaknesses: The baseline evaluation is too narrow to substantiate the benchmark's central claims. Only PPO with MLP and LSTM backbones is evaluated. A benchmark explicitly motivated by comparing 'memory mechanisms' across agents should include at least a few modern memory architectures (e.g., transformer-based policies such as GTrXL, state-space models like S4/Mamba variants, or retrieval-based agents such as R2A/AdaMemento), several of which are discussed in Table 2 but never actually run. With only LSTM as the sole representative of memory-enhanced agents, the benchmark's discriminative power across memory mechanisms remains unverified.

MIKASA-Base is presented as a headline contribution, but no experiments are reported on it. The paper proposes a unified suite of ~25 existing environments yet provides zero baseline results, cross-agent comparisons, or validation on this suite; its value as a contribution is thus asserted rather than demonstrated. As it stands, MIKASA-Base is largely a re-packaging of existing environments (POPGym, BSuite, MemoryGym, Memory Maze, etc.) under one API.

The taxonomy, while useful, is somewhat coarse and its boundaries are fuzzy: many tasks are assigned to two categories (e.g., 'Sequential, Object', 'Capacity, Sequential'), and assignments appear largely subjective with no validation (no inter-annotator agreement, no demonstration that the categories predict distinct agent failure profiles). The claimed 'comprehensive' classification is difficult to verify against formal criteria.

Several results are problematic rather than informative: under sparse rewards essentially everything fails for both architectures, and both MLP and LSTM fail on medium/hard difficulty with dense rewards. Without at least one agent that partially solves these settings, it is unclear whether the hard variants are well-calibrated tests of memory or simply too difficult/under-shaped for current methods (e.g., exploration failures masquerading as memory failures). The paper interprets total failure as 'revealing the true challenge', which is a charitable reading that needs more evidence.

The robotics tasks, while nicely designed, share a fairly homogeneous structure (phase-based observe-then-act with occlusion/delay) and many differ only in surface parameters (number of colors, number of cups, angle ranges). The claimed diversity across '12 categories' partly reflects parameter variations rather than fundamentally distinct memory challenges.

No experiments connect the taxonomy to the robotics results: the paper does not show, e.g., that an agent good at Object Memory tasks is systematically worse at Sequential Memory tasks. This would be the key validation of the classification framework and its premise that 'task-specific strengths remain hidden' under narrow evaluation.

Some overclaiming relative to evidence: phrases like 'driving the development of more reliable systems for real-world applications' and 'comprehensive benchmark' exceed what PPO-LSTM failure curves on simulated tabletop tasks support; no sim-to-real considerations or discussion of the simulators' fidelity to 'real-world' memory demands.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: memory evaluation in RL is fragmented, and there is no standardized memory-intensive benchmark for robotic manipulation (Table 2/3 survey of existing benchmarks and frameworks is thorough and useful).

Substantial and complete resource: MIKASA-Robo provides 32 tasks across 12 categories on ManiSkill3 (GPU-parallelizable, unlike RLBench-based MemoryBench), plus offline datasets, trained agent weights, collection scripts, and pip-installable package — good reproducibility (Appendices A-B, G).

Careful benchmark validation methodology: PPO-MLP trained in state mode achieving 100% success rate across all tasks (Figures 7-8) convincingly demonstrates the tasks are well-calibrated and solvable, so failures in partial-observability modes are attributable to memory/learning limitations rather than task design flaws.

Breadth of evaluation: online RL (PPO-MLP/LSTM, SAC, TD-MPC2), offline RL (BC, CQL, DT, RATE, Diffusion Policy), and VLA models (Octo, OpenVLA) across dense/sparse reward settings; results clearly show performance degradation with memory demands, validating the benchmark's difficulty gradient (3/5/9 complexity levels).

Interesting empirical findings, e.g., action chunking in OpenVLA partially bypassing memory requirements, and near-total failure of all offline methods on capacity/sequential tasks, which are useful signals for the community.
weaknesses: The proposed taxonomy (object/spatial/sequential/capacity) is fairly coarse, overlaps substantially with prior classifications (e.g., Cherepanov et al. [9], Ni et al. [68]), and its boundaries are not rigorously defined or empirically validated — several tasks are assigned to multiple categories in Table 7, suggesting the four categories are not cleanly separated.
MIKASA-Base is largely a re-packaging/wrapper of existing environments (POPGym, BSuite, Memory Maze, MemoryGym, etc.) under a common API; its novelty is limited to consolidation.

Weak coverage of strong modern memory architectures: only PPO-LSTM and transformer-based offline models (DT/RATE) are evaluated; no GTrXL, AMAGO, world-model-based agents (Dreamer), or state-space models are tested. As a result, the paper's central claim that the benchmark 'enables objective evaluation of memory mechanisms' and can distinguish between architectures is only demonstrated at the MLP-vs-LSTM level.

Potential confound between memory difficulty and low-level control difficulty: tasks like ShellGamePick, InterceptGrab, and RotateStrict involve significant dexterity challenges, so failures may stem from motor control rather than memory; the paper does not disentangle these factors (e.g., no control experiments testing memory-less agents with oracle memory hints).

Evaluation completeness gaps: only a subset of tasks is shown for VLA and some online baselines; offline results show exactly 0.00 success on 9 of 32 tasks for all five methods, raising the concern that parts of the benchmark may currently be unsolvable with available data/budget (1000 trajectories), limiting its usefulness as a progress-tracking tool; no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis is provided for the offline baselines.

VLA experiments are admittedly under-tuned (limited fine-tuning), so conclusions about VLA memory capabilities are tentative; sparse-reward online results appear in the appendix with limited analysis.

Writing quality issues: grammatical errors ('utilize his historical information', 'presents am ordered sequence', 'BEHAVIOR-1k' vs 'BEHAVIOR-1K'), and some claims (e.g., taxonomy being 'comprehensive') are stronger than the supporting argument.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: there is no standardized benchmark for memory capabilities in robotic manipulation, and the paper makes a substantial engineering effort (32 tasks, 12 categories, released datasets for offline RL, pip-installable package, code examples) that is likely useful to the community.

Reasonable validation methodology for task solvability: PPO-MLP with full state access achieves 100% success across all tasks, supporting the claim that task failures under partial observability stem from memory/algorithm limitations rather than broken environments.

Breadth of baseline evaluation is a plus: online RL (PPO-MLP/LSTM, SAC, TD-MPC2), offline RL (DT, RATE, BC, CQL, DP), and VLA models (Octo, OpenVLA) are evaluated, including an interesting analysis of action chunking as an imperfect substitute for memory in VLAs.
The related-work survey (Tables 2 and 3) cataloguing which memory environments and robotics frameworks prior work used is thorough and could be a useful reference.
Detailed task documentation in the appendix (reward structures, success criteria, observation modes) supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core contributions. MIKASA-Base is essentially a repackaging of existing open-source environments (POPGym, BSuite, Memory Maze, Memory Gym, Minigrid, ViZDoom) under a common Gymnasium API; no new environments are introduced there. The four-way taxonomy (object/spatial/sequential/capacity) is straightforward and overlaps substantially with prior classifications (e.g., Cherepanov et al.), which the paper itself acknowledges; the cognitive-science framing is largely motivational rather than a rigorous formal contribution.

The benchmark's ability to differentiate memory mechanisms is weakly demonstrated. On the hardest tasks, all baselines — including memory-based ones like PPO-LSTM, RATE, and DT — fail with near-zero success rates (entire rows of 0.00 in Table 6, and near-zero across the board with sparse rewards in Figure 10). When everything fails, the benchmark measures difficulty but provides little signal about memory capabilities; this resembles 'we built tasks no one can solve' rather than a diagnostic instrument.

Confounding of memory difficulty with exploration/control difficulty. Sparse-reward manipulation is hard for all methods regardless of memory demands; the paper does not convincingly isolate that failures are attributable to memory rather than to exploration, perception, or credit assignment. Only the state-vs-RGB+joints contrast partially addresses this, and it is shown for a limited subset of tasks.

Task-to-taxonomy assignment appears ad hoc in places (e.g., Intercept tasks are arguably more about velocity estimation/trajectory prediction than memory per se; BunchOfColors vs. SeqOfColors distinctions are thin), and no principled procedure or quantitative validation of the classification is provided.

Only three training runs per baseline; given the high variance visible in several curves (e.g., TakeItBack, InterceptGrabSlow), the reliability of reported differences is questionable. Several baseline settings also appear under-tuned (e.g., OpenVLA K=4 fails 'across the board', attributed only to limited fine-tuning).

MIKASA-Base is not evaluated empirically in the paper: no baseline results are reported for it, so its claim of 'unified evaluation' is asserted rather than demonstrated. The main experimental weight rests on MIKASA-Robo.

Positioning relative to the concurrent MemoryBench is somewhat dismissive (three tasks, spatial only) without head-to-head comparison, and the paper's own claim of being 'the first systematic and unified benchmark' is weakened by prior and concurrent work.

Writing quality is uneven (e.g., repeated DebugRewardWrapper() description in Appendix A, minor grammatical issues, inconsistency between 'Table 2' referenced before it appears), and key details such as hyperparameter sensitivity or compute budgets for the many baselines are scattered.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clearly-articulated gap: memory evaluation in RL is fragmented, and there is no standardized memory-intensive benchmark for robotic manipulation. The motivation and related-work analysis (Tables 1-3) convincingly document this fragmentation.

MIKASA-Robo is a substantial and carefully engineered contribution: 32 tasks across 12 categories, built on ManiSkill3 with GPU-parallel training, multiple observation modes (state/RGB/joints/oracle/prompt), and both dense and sparse reward variants. This flexibility supports systematic memory-focused study.

Good benchmark validation methodology: the authors demonstrate tasks are solvable at 100% success rate by a PPO-MLP agent with full state access (Figures 4, 7-8), which rules out inherent task-design flaws and strengthens the claim that observed failures in RGB+joints mode stem from memory limitations rather than unsolvable environments.

Comprehensive baseline coverage spanning three paradigms: online RL (PPO-MLP/LSTM, SAC, TD-MPC2), offline RL (DT, RATE, BC, CQL, DP) with released datasets of 1000 trajectories per task, and VLA models (Octo, OpenVLA). The experiments consistently show performance degradation with increasing memory demands, validating the benchmark's discriminative power.
Strong reproducibility: pip-installable package, released datasets, dataset collection scripts, agent weights, and detailed implementation documentation in the appendix.
The paper is clearly written, well organized, and the detailed per-task appendix (Section H) makes the benchmark easy to understand and use.
weaknesses: The four-category taxonomy (object, spatial, sequential, capacity) is relatively coarse and its assignments appear partly subjective; several tasks could plausibly belong to multiple categories (e.g., Intercept involves velocity estimation and credit assignment as much as spatial memory). The taxonomy is asserted rather than empirically validated with architecture-level analysis.

Evaluation of memory architectures is shallow relative to the paper's claims. The only memory-enhanced online baseline is PPO-LSTM; well-known stronger memory agents (GTrXL, R2D2/RECURREN-style, AMAGO, world models like Dreamer, SSM-based agents) listed in Table 2 are not evaluated on MIKASA-Robo. The claim that the benchmark can distinguish different memory utilization patterns (Figure 1's central promise) is therefore only weakly supported.

Many baselines achieve near-zero performance on large fractions of the benchmark (all offline methods score 0.00 on 9 tasks; online sparse-reward experiments fail almost everywhere). This raises the question of whether the difficulty reflects memory requirements or confounds such as sparse-reward exploration difficulty, reward shaping, or visual representation learning; the paper does not fully disentangle these factors.
MIKASA-Base is largely a repackaging of existing open-source environments under a common API; its novelty is limited to curation and categorization.
Only three training seeds are used per configuration, limiting statistical robustness, particularly for the offline comparisons where differences are often small relative to the SEM.
The VLA study is limited to a small task subset and admittedly under-tuned models; conclusions about chunk-size effects (K=4 vs K=8) are drawn from sparse evidence.

All experiments are simulation-only; while the tasks are motivated by real-world robotic memory needs, no sim-to-real or even high-fidelity realism evidence is provided, so claims about 'real-world use' are aspirational.
Comparison with the concurrent MemoryBench is limited to prose claims; a direct empirical head-to-head on overlapping tasks would strengthen the positioning.
